module_title: Vijayanagara and Bahmani - Economy, Factionalism, Diplomacy, and Decline
introduction: At this advanced level, we analyze the Vijayanagara economy (currency system), the unique status of women, the political symbolism of the Mahanavami Dibba, the destructive Afaqui-Dakhni factionalism within the Bahmani court, and the nuanced diplomacy that led to the Battle of Talikota.

core_concepts.title: Economy, Trade, and Currency
core_concepts.description: Vijayanagara was immensely prosperous, dominating the spice and textile trade. They imported Arabian horses extensively via the Portuguese. Their standard gold coin was called 'Varaha' (referred to as 'Pagoda' or 'Huna' by foreigners).

core_concepts.title: Political Symbolism of the Mahanavami Dibba
core_concepts.description: The 'Mahanavami Dibba' in Hampi was not just a religious platform; it served a deep political purpose. Here, Amara-Nayakas presented gifts and tribute to the King, publicly reaffirming the monarch's suzerainty.

core_concepts.title: Society and Status of Women
core_concepts.description: Vijayanagara is noted for the exceptionally diverse roles of women in medieval India. Accounts of Nuniz confirm that women were employed as wrestlers, astrologers, accountants, and even royal bodyguards.

core_concepts.title: Afaqui vs. Dakhni Factionalism
core_concepts.description: The Bahmani court was fatally paralyzed by the rivalry between 'Afaquis' (foreign immigrant Muslims from Iran/Turkey) and 'Dakhnis' (local Muslims and converts). This factionalism led to the unjust execution of Mahmud Gawan and the empire's ultimate disintegration.

core_concepts.title: Diplomacy Leading to Talikota (1565)
core_concepts.description: Rama Raya (the de facto ruler of Vijayanagara) employed a divisive foreign policy, playing the Deccan Sultanates against each other. Eventually, realizing the threat, Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, and Bidar formed a grand alliance against Vijayanagara. Notably, 'Berar' did not join.

important_entities.name: Rama Raya
important_entities.key_fact: De facto ruler during the Aravidu Dynasty
important_entities.significance: His overconfident and manipulative diplomacy led to the formation of the Deccan Confederacy. He was captured and beheaded at the Battle of Talikota.

important_entities.name: Caesar Frederick
important_entities.significance: He visited Vijayanagara immediately after the Battle of Talikota (1567) and documented the tragic ruin and desolation of the once-great capital.

important_entities.name: Amara-Nayakas
important_entities.significance: Given territories (Amaram) to govern in exchange for providing a stipulated number of troops to the king. It was conceptually similar to the 'Iqta' system of the Delhi Sultanate.

important_entities.name: Gol Gumbaz
important_entities.significance: The mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah of the Adil Shahi dynasty. It boasts one of the largest single-chamber domes in the world and features a famous 'whispering gallery'.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Who was NOT in the Talikota Confederacy?
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: This is a frequent and tricky UPSC-level question. Out of the 5 Deccan Sultanates, 'Berar' did not participate in the Battle of Talikota against Vijayanagara due to its bitter enmity with Golconda.
Since the empire was in the deep south, students often guess Tamil or Kannada as the language of the king's masterpiece. Amuktamalyada is, in fact, an epic poem written in 'Telugu'.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Match them conceptually: Golconda sounds like Qutb (Minar); Ahmadnagar was ruled by Nizam Shahis (don't confuse with Nizams of Hyderabad).
Use the wordplay that 'Berar' was 'barred' (kept out) of the grand alliance at Talikota.

exam_strategy_tips: For advanced exams (like UPSC/State PCS), expect analytical, statement-based questions comparing the 'Nayankara' system with the 'Iqta' or 'Mansabdari' systems.
Pay close attention to Vijayanagara's advanced water management systems (like the Kamalapuram tank and elaborate canal networks) mentioned by foreign travellers.
